I looked from one to the other, smiling, defiant.
“Why, Bob said she was a pale, pinched-up snippet of a thing with golden hair,” whispered a slip of a girl to a smooth little woman at her side.
“Ay, my Goff! And a waist like a wedding-ring,” responded a wide mouth in a large red face, peering over.
“Ah, lady,” warbled the Signorina, “fair today and foul tomorrow. ‘Believe what you are told,’ clanked the bell in the churchyard. Stuffing, my pretty; ask the goose!”
So went the Signorina’s last little orgy. It would be a lie to profess that she, or rather some black hidden ghost in her, did not enjoy it. My monstrous disguise, that ferment of humanity, those owlish faces, the lurking shame, the danger, the poisonous excitement swept me clean out of myself. Anything to be free for a while from “pernickety” Miss M. But that, I suppose, is the experience of every gambler and wastrel and jezebel in the world, every one of his kind. One must not open the door too wide.
But this was not all. On other nights I had been alone. Now I was fervidly conscious of unseen, hungering eyes, watching every turn, and glance, and gesture. My dingy dais was no longer in actuality. I lived in that one watcher’s mind﻿—in his imagination. And deep beneath this insane excitement lay a gentle, longing happiness. Oh, when this vile tinsel show was over, and these swarming faces had melted into thin air, and the moonlit empty night was ours, what would I not pour out for his peace and comfort. What gratitude and tenderness for all that he had been to me, and done, and said. Why, we seemed never even to have spoken to each other﻿—not self to self, and there was all the world to tell.
Hotter, ranker grew the fetid atmosphere. I could scarcely breathe in my monstrous mummery. But clearly, the showman was making a rich bargain of me, and rumour of a Midget that was golden as Aphrodite one night, and black as pitch the next, only thickened the swarm. At length﻿—long expected﻿—there came a pause. Yet another country urchin flat on his stomach in the grass, with head goggling up at me from the hem of the canvas, was dragged out, screeching and laughing, by his breeches. But I had caught the accents of a well-known voice, and, crouching, with head wrenched aside to listen, I heard the gipsy’s whining reply.
My moment had come. A pulse began its tattoo in my head.

===Chinese===

我从一张脸望到另一张脸，笑着，挑衅着。
“咦，鲍勃不是说，她是个苍白干瘪的小不点儿，一头金发嘛，”一个瘦条条姑娘悄声对她身旁圆顺的小妇人说。
“可不是嘛，老天！腰细得跟结婚戒指似的，”一张大红脸上咧着的宽嘴探过头来应道。
“哎，太太，”瑟诺莉娜莺声道，“今日天晴明日雨。‘人家说啥你信啥’，墓园里的钟当啷说。肚里的干货嘛，小可爱；去问问鹅！”
瑟诺莉娜最后一场小小的狂欢，就这样过去了。若说她——或者说她体内某个幽黑的鬼——不曾享受它，那是撒谎。我那骇人的伪装、那发酵的人潮、那些猫头鹰般的脸、潜伏的羞耻、危险、带毒的兴奋，把我整个卷出了自身。哪怕只一时半刻，能逃离“斤斤计较”的M小姐，怎样都行。可这，我想，也是世间每个赌徒、浪子、荡妇的经历，每个这一类人的经历。那扇门，不可开得太大。
但还不止此。别的夜晚，我总是独自一人。此刻我却灼灼地觉出一只看不见的、饥渴的眼睛，守着我的一颦一动、一姿一势。我那昏暗的小台，不再真实。我活在那位守望者的心里——活在他的想象里。而这疯狂的兴奋底下，静静躺着一份温柔的、渴盼的幸福。哦，等这俗艳的廉价戏收场，这些人潮的面孔化入空无，月下空寂的夜归我们所有，为了他的安宁与安适，我还有什么不肯倾吐的。为了他之于我的一切、他所做、他所说，该有多少感激与柔情。说来，我们竟像还从未真正交谈过——不曾以本真对本真——而有整个世界可讲。
浊热的空气愈发腥秽。裹在这副骇人的行头里，我几乎透不过气。可显然，班主正拿我做一笔肥买卖；而“侏儒一夜金如阿芙洛狄忒，转夜黑如沥青”的传闻，只让人越围越厚。终于——盼了许久——来了一个间歇。又一个乡下顽童趴在草里、从帆布边沿探头瞪我，被人拤着裤腰拖了出去，尖叫着、大笑着。可我已辨出一个熟悉的嗓音的口音；我蜷起身子，把头扭向一边细听，听见了吉卜赛女人呜呜咽咽的回话。
我的时刻到了。一记脉搏开始在我头里敲起鼓点。

===Original===

To remain helplessly lying there was impossible. I thrust myself on to my feet and, drawing back a pace or two, stood hunched up on the crimson spread of satin beside my wooden bolster. The canvas lifted, and one by one, the little party of “gentry” stooped and filed in.

===Chinese===

无助地赖在那里，是不可能的。我攋起身子，退后一两步，佝偻着立在猩红绸缎的铺面上、我的木枕旁边。帆布掀起，一小队“贵客”躬着身，鱼贯而入。

### LII / LII
===Original===

Mrs. Monnerie had paid for elbow room. It was the last “Private View” in this world we were to share together. The sight of her capacious figure with its great bonnet and the broad, dark face beneath, now suddenly become strange and hostile, filled me with a vague sense of desolation. Yet I know she has forgiven me. Had I not pocketed my “pretty little fastidiousness”?
What Fanny had planned to do if Miss M., plain and simple, had occupied the Signorina’s table I cannot even guess. For the spectacle of the squat, black, gloating guy she actually found there, she was utterly unprepared. It seemed, as I looked at her, that myself had fainted﻿—had withdrawn out of my body﻿—like the spirit in sleep. Or, maybe, not to be too nice about it, I merely “became” my disguise. With mind emptied of every thought, I sank into an almost lifeless stagnancy, and with a heavy settled stare out of my black and yellow, from under the coarse fringe that brushed my brows, I met her eyes. Out of time and place, in a lightless, vacant solitude, we wrestled for mastery. At length the sneering, incredulous smile slowly faded from the pale, lovely face, leaving it twisted up as if after a nauseous draught of physic. Her gaze faltered, and fell. Her bosom rose; she coughed and turned away.
“Hideous! monstrous!” murmured Mrs. Monnerie to the tall, expressionless figure that stood beside her. “The abject evil of the creature!”
Her dark, appraising glance travelled over me﻿—feet, hands, body, lace-draped head. It swept across my eyes as if they were less significant than bits of china stuck in a coconut.
“No, Miss Bowater,” she turned massively round on her, “you were perfectly right, it seems. As usual﻿—but a dangerous habit, my dear. My little ransoming scheme must wait a bit. Just as well, perhaps, that our patient’s dainty nerves should have been spared this particular little initiation﻿—. Could one have imagined it?”
Mr. Padgwick-Steggall merely raised his eyebrows. “I shouldn’t have cared to try,” he drawled. And the lady beside him made a little mouth and laid her gloved hand on his arm.
“But, Madame is forgetting,” whined the Signorina in a broken nosy English over her outspread fan, “Madame is forgetting. It’s alive! Oh, truly!” and I clasped my arms even tighter across my padded chest, my body involuntarily rocking to and fro, though not with amusement.

===Chinese===

莫纳里太太花钱包下了专场。这是我们在人世共度的最后一场「预展」。望着她那宽阔的身影、那顶大软帽和帽下宽阔黝黑的脸——此刻骤然变得陌生而敌对——我心里漫起一阵茫然的荒凉。然而我知道，她已原谅了我。我不是把那点「精致的小挑剔」装进口袋了吗？
倘若今晚占着西尼奥里娜（Signorina）台子的，是清清爽爽、素面朝天的M小姐（Miss M.），范妮打算怎么办——这我连猜也猜不出。因为她实际见到的那副景象——一个蹲坐的、涂黑的、目光贪婪的假人——她全无心理准备。我望着她，仿佛我自己晕了过去——从躯壳里退了出去——像睡梦中的魂灵。或者，不必说得太细，我只是「变成了」我的伪装。心里掣空了一切念头，我沉入一种近乎无生的滞钝，从粗刘海底下，用我那黑黄相间的一双眼睛，沉沉定定地迎住她的目光。出了时，出了空，在一处无光无人的孤寂里，我们角力着争胜。终于，那苍白可爱的脸上讥消的、不敢相信的笑慢慢褪尽了，只剩下五官扭作一团，仿佛刚灌下一剂令人作呕的药。她的目光乱了，垂了。她胸脯一起伏，咳嗽一声，转过脸去。
「丑极了！怪极了！」莫纳里太太对她身旁那个高挑而无表情的身影咕哝道。「这东西下贱得恶毒！」
她那双幽黑的、估价的目光把我巡视了一遍——脚、手、身子、蒙着花边纱的头。它扫过我的双眼，仿佛它们还比不上嵌在椰壳上的两片瓷。
「不，鲍沃特小姐，」她大身子缓缓转向她，「看来您说得一点不错。一如既往——不过这习惯可危险哪，亲爱的。我那小小的赎人计划只好缓一缓了。也好，说不定——免得咱们那位病人的娇神经再受这场小小的入门礼——。谁想得到呢？」
帕奇威克-斯特加尔先生只扬了扬眉。「换了我可不愿一试，」他慢吞吞地说。他身旁那位女士撇了撇嘴，把戴手套的手搭上他的手臂。
「可是，夫人忘了，」西尼奥里娜隔着摊开的扇子，用蹩脚的、鼻音浓重的英语哀声说，「夫人忘了。它是活的哟！哦，真的！」我把双臂在塞得鼓鼓的胸前搂得更紧，身子不由自主地前后摇晃——虽然并非出于快活。

===Original===

“Madame is forgetting nothing of the kind,” retorted Mrs. Monnerie heartily. “The princess is an angel﻿—Angélique﻿—adorable.” She turned to the gipsy woman and slipped a coin into the clawlike fingers. “Well, good night,” she nodded at me. “We are perfectly satisfied.”
“La, la, Madame,” my stuttering voice called after her, the words leaping out from some old hiding-place in my mind. “*Je vous remercie, madame. Rien ne va plus.﻿ ﻿… Noir gagne!*”
Her ebony stick shook beneath her hand. “Unspeakable,” she angrily ejaculated, stumping her way out. “A positive outrage against humanity.”
I shut my eyes, but the silent laughter that had once overtaken me in my bedroom at Mrs. Bowater’s scarcely sounded in my head. And Mrs. Monnerie could more easily survive the little exchange than I. My body was dull and aching as if after a severe fall. The booth was filling for the last time.
Little life was left in the inert figure that faced this new assortment of her fellow-creatures: how strangely dissimilar one from another; how horrifyingly alike. A faint premonition bade me be on my guard. Under the wavering flame of the lamp, my glance moved slowly on from face to face, eye on to eye; and behind everyone a watcher whom now I dared not wait to challenge. Empty or cynical, disgusted, malevolent, or blankly curious, they met me: none pitiful; none saddened or afflicted. On former nights﻿—Why had they grown so hostile? This, then, was to smother in the bog.
But one face there was known to me, and that known well. Hoping, perhaps, to take me unaware, or may it have been to snatch a secret word with me; Fanny had slipped back into the tent again, and was now steadily regarding me from behind the throng. A throng so densely packed together that the canvas walls bulged behind them, and the tent-pole bent beneath the strain. Yet so much alone were she and I in that last infinite moment that we might have been whispering together after death. And this time, suddenly overwhelmed with self-loathing, it was I who turned away.
When, stretching my cramped limbs, I drew back, exhausted and shivering, from the empty tent, I thought for an instant that the figure which sat crouching in the corner of the recess was asleep. But no: with head averted, sweat gleaming on his forehead, he rose to his feet. His consciousness had been my theatre in a degree past even my realization.

===Chinese===

「夫人什么也没忘，」莫纳里太太热辣辣地回敬。「这位公主是个天使——安杰莉克——可爱极了。」她转向那吉普赛女人，把一枚硬币塞进她爪子般的手指间。「好吧，晚安，」她朝我点点头。「我们十二分满意。」
「啦，啦，夫人，」我结结巴巴的嗓音在她背后响起，那些字眼从我脑海里某个藏了很久的旮旯里蹦了出来。「*Je vous remercie, madame. Rien ne va plus. … Noir gagne!*（谢谢您，夫人。停止下注。……黑方赢了！）」
她乌木手杖在掌下直颤。「不堪言说，」她怒冲冲地迸出一句，咚咚地顿着杖出去了。「对人类的公然冒犯。」
我闭上眼，可当年在鲍沃特太太卧室里攫住我的那种无声的笑，此刻在我脑中几乎响不起来。何况，同莫纳里太太相比，我更不容易从这场小小的交锋里全身而退。我的身子又钝又痛，仿佛狠狠摔了一跤。棚子最后一次满了起来。
面对这一批新凑拢的同类，那具呆滞的身影里已剩不下多少生气：人与人何其异样地互不相同；又何其骇人地彼此相像。一丝模糊的预感告诫我警惕。在摇曳的灯光下，我的目光缓缓地一张脸一张脸移过去，一双眼睛一双眼睛望过去；每张脸背后都立着一个窥视者，此刻我已不敢等下去与他对质。空洞的，或玩世的，憎厌的，恶毒的，或全然好奇的，它们迎着我：没有一张怜悯；没有一张哀伤或悲恸。先前的那些夜里——他们怎么变得这样敌对了？原来，这就是沉入泥沼窒息的感觉。
可有一张脸是我认得的，而且认得很熟。也许是想乘我不备，也许——谁知道呢——是想同我偷说一句体己话：范妮又溜回了帐篷，正从人堆后面定定地望着我。人堆挤得那样密，身后的帆布壁都鼓了起来，帐杆都被压得弯了。可在那最后的无边的一刻里，她和我又是那样孤单，孤单得仿佛死后还在彼此耳语。而这一回，突然被自我厌憎淹没、转过脸去的，是我。
等我伸展僵麻的四肢，拖着疲惫与寒战，从空下来的帐篷里退出来，有一瞬我以为蜷在帷幄角落里的人影睡着了。却不是：他偏着头，额上汗光闪闪，站起身来。他这一路的意识，一直是我的一座剧场，其程度之深，连我自己都不曾察觉。

===Original===

“Then, that is over,” was all he said. “Now it is my turn.”
The voice was flat and indifferent, but he could not conceal his disgust of what had passed, nor his dread of what was to come. Why, I thought angrily once more as I looked at him, why did he exaggerate things like this? Even a drowning man can sink three times, and still cheat the water. What cared I?﻿—the night was nearly over. We should have won release. Why consider it so deeply? But even while I pleaded with him to let me finish the wretched business﻿—every savour of adventure and daring and romance gone from it now﻿—I was conscious of the trussed-up monstrosity that confronted him. He could not endure even a glance at my painted face. I stepped back from him with a hidden grimace. Past even praying for, then. So be it.
I heard the nimble stepping of the pony’s hoofs on the worn turf. A sullen malice smouldered in its reddish, luminous eyes. When I clutched at its bridle it jerked back its sensitive head as if teased with a gadfly. The gipsy daubed vermilion on my friend’s sallow cheeks. She shook out the tarnished finery she had brought with her and hung it round the stooping shoulders. She plastered down his black hair above his eyes, and thrust a riding-whip into his hand.
“There, my fine pretty gentleman,” she smirked at him. “King of the Carrots! I lay even your own mammie wouldn’t know you now, not even if you tried it straddle-legs. Tug at the knot, lovey; it’s fast, but it won’t strangle you. As for you, you﻿—!” she suddenly flamed at me, “all very fly and cunning, but if I’d had the fixing of it, you wouldn’t have diddled me: not you. I know *your* shop. Slick off double quick, I warn you, or you’ll have the mob at your heels. Now then, master!”
She grasped at the bridle, slapped the tooth-bared sensitive muzzle with her hand. I drew back, cowed and speechless. The sour thought died in my mind﻿—Better, perhaps, if we had missed each other on the road. The pony jerked and snatched back its head.
---
He was gone, and now I was quite alone. What was there to fear? Only his contempt, his loathing of this last humiliation? But that, too, would soon be nothing but a memory. As always, the present would glide into the past. Yet a dreadful foreboding daunted me. Coarse canvas, walls and roof, table, beaten grass, my very hands and clothes had become menacing and unreal.

===Chinese===

「那么，那一场完了，」他只说了这一句。「现在轮到我。」
嗓音平直而冷淡，可他掩不住对方才种种的憎恶，也掩不住对将临之事的恐惧。为什么，我望着他又一次恼火地想，为什么他把事情夸张成这样？就连溺水的人也能沉三次，还能骗过水。我管它呢？——夜快完了。我们就要赢得解脱了。何必想得这么深？可就在我恳求他让我把这桩倒霉的营生做完的时候——那里面冒险、胆气与传奇的滋味如今已荡然无存——我也意识到，同他面对面的，是怎样一副捆扎起来的怪物。连看一眼我这张涂画的脸，他都受不住。我藏着个鬼脸，从他身边退开。连求也不必求了。那就这样吧。
我听见矮马的蹄子踏上磨损的草皮，步子轻捷。它那双泛红的亮眼里闷烧着愠怒的恶意。我去抓它的笼头，它猛地甩回那敏感的头，仿佛被牛虻揽扰。吉普赛女人往我朋友蜡黄的脸上涂抹朱红。她抖开带来的那身黯旧的行头，披上他佝偻的双肩。她把他眼睛上面的黑发抹平，把一根马鞭塞进他手里。
「瞧，我的漂亮阔少爷，」她朝他假笑。「胡萝卜王！我看这会儿连你亲妈也认不得你啦，任你叉开腿装也没用。拽拽那个结儿，宝贝；打得紧，可勒不死你。至于你，你——！」她忽然冲我发起火来，「鬼精鬼灵的，可要是由我来安排，你甭想蒙我：你甭想。*你*那家铺子我清楚。麻利点儿赶紧开溜，我警告你，不然暴民要追你的脚后跟了。来吧，爷！」
她抓住笼头，一巴掌拍在那號着牙的敏感口鼻上。我畏缩后退，噤若寒蝉。心里那股酸涩的念头死掉了——兴许，路上彼此错过反倒好。矮马一颠，又猛地夺回了头。
---
他走了，如今我孤身一人。还有什么可怕的呢？无非是他的轻蔑，他对这最后一桩羞辱的憎厌？可那也很快将不过是一段记忆。一如既往，现在自会滑成过去。然而一种可怕的预感使我胆寒。粗帆布，四壁与顶棚，桌子，踩塌的草，连我自己的手和衣裳，都变得凶险而不真实。

===Original===

The lamp hissed and bubbled as if at any moment it would burst asunder. Alone, afraid, ashamed, in the foulness of the tent, I looked around me in the silence; and beyond, above﻿—the Universe of night and space. All my life but the feeble rustlings of a mouse in straw.
As I stripped off my miserable gewgaws I discovered myself talking into my solitude; weeping, beseeching, though eyes were dry and tongue silent. I scoured away the chalk and paint: and cleansed as far as possible my travel-stained clothes. From my bit of looking-glass a scared and shining face looked out. “Oh, my dear,” I whispered, but not to its reflection, “it is as clean now and forever as I can make it.” I tied up my bundle.
It was impossible to cheat away the moments any longer. I sat down and listened. A distant roar of welcome, like that of a wave breaking over a wreck, had been borne across as the band broke into its welcoming tune. I saw the ring, its tall, lank-cheeked “master” in his white shirt and coattails, the lights, the sidling, squalling clown, and the slim, exquisite creature with its ungainly rider ambling on and on. Where sat Fanny amidst that rabble? What were her thoughts? Was Mrs. Monnerie already yawning over the low, beggarly scene? A few minutes now. I began to count. A scream, human or animal, rose faint and awful in the distance, and died away.
I climbed down the ladder and looked out of the tent. Far-spread the fields and wooded hills lay, as if in a swoon beneath the blazing moonlight. The scattered lamps on the slope shone dim as glowworms. Only a few figures loitered in the gleam of the sideshows, and so engrossed and still sat the watching multitude beneath the enormous mushroom of the tent, so thinly floated out its strains of music, that the hollow clucking of the stream over its pebbles beneath the wan-stoned bridge was audible. A few isolated stars glittered faintly in the heights of the sky. What was happening now? Why did he not hasten? I was ready: my life prepared. I could bear no more waiting. A whip cracked. The music ceased: silence. One moment now.
Again the whip cracked. And then, as if at a signal, a vast, protracted, unanimous bawl poured up into space, a spout of sound, like a gigantic, invisible flower. “That wasn’t applause. But, you know, that wasn’t applause,” I heard myself muttering.

===Chinese===

油灯嘶嘶地冒着泡，仿佛随时要炸裂开来。孤单，害怕，羞惭，置身于帐篷的污浊里，我在寂静中环顾四周；而更远处、更高处——是夜与空间的宇宙。我这一生，不过是稻草里一只老鼠的窸窣。
剥下那一身可怜的花哨玩意儿时，我发现自己在对着孤寂说话；哭泣着，哀告着，尽管眼睛是干的，舌头是哑的。我把白垩和油彩擦刮干净：又把风尘仆仆的衣裳尽量收拾了。小镜子里探出一张惊惶而光洁的脸。「哦，亲爱的，」我轻声说，却不是说给镜中人，「如今它已经干净了，而且永远干净，尽我所能了。」我把包襁系好。
再也没法把此刻搪塞过去了。我坐下细听。乐队奏起迎客的曲子时，远处传来一阵欢迎的吼声，像浪头砸上失事船。我看见那圆场：瘦长脸颊的「班主」穿着白衬衫和燕尾服，灯彩，侧身挪步、哇哇怪叫的小丑，还有那匹纤秀俊美的小兽驮着笨拙的骑手，一圈一圈地溜着蹄。范妮坐在那群乌合之众中间的哪儿？她想些什么？莫纳里太太是否已对着这低贱寒酸的场面打起呵欠？就剩几分钟了。我开始数数。一声尖叫，分不清是人还是兽，在远处微弱而可怕地升起，又消逝。
我爬下梯凳，朝帐篷外张望。田帲和树木葱茏的山丘远远铺展，仿佛在炽亮的月光下晕了过去。坡上零星的灯火暗得像萤火虫。只有几个人影还在杂耍棚的光亮边闲荡；帐幕那朵巨菌底下，围观的众人坐得那样出神、那样安静，音乐那样轻薄地飘散出来，以致灰白石桥下溪水漫过卵石的空洞的淙淙声都听得见。高天上几颗孤星幽幽闪烁。此刻进行到哪儿了？他为什么还不快点？我已就绪：一生都收拾停当。再等不下去了。鞭子一响。乐声止了：寂静。就是此刻了。
鞭子又是一响。随即，仿佛一声令下，一片浩大的、绵延的、万众齐发的吼啸灌入夜空，一柱声音的喷泉，像一朵巨大而无形的花。「那不是喝彩。可是你知道，那不是喝彩，」我听见自己喃喃。

===Original===

There can be no mistaking the sound of human mockery. There can be no mistaking that brutal wrench at the heart, under one’s very ribs. I leapt round where I stood, in a kind of giddiness.
The shout died away. An indiscriminate clamour broke out﻿—clapping of hands, beating of feet, whistling, hootings, booings, catcalls, and these all but drowned by cymbal, drum, trombone: “Goodbye, Sweetheart, Goodbye.” It was over. Unlike Mrs. Monnerie, the mob was imperfectly satisfied. But all was well. The elephant, massive, imperturbable﻿—the sagacious elephant with the hurdy-gurdy, must now be swinging into the ring.
I ran out over the trampled grass to meet the approaching group﻿—showman, gipsy, trembling, sweating pony. Its rider stooped forward on the saddle, clutching its pommel, as if afraid of falling. He pushed himself off, lurched unsteadily, lifted and let fall his arm in an attempt to stroke the milk-white snapping muzzle. The strings of his cloak were already broken. He edged from beneath it, and with his left hand clumsily brushed the dust and damp from his face.
“He hadn’t quite the knack of it,” the showman was explaining. “Stirrup a morsel too short, maybe. All the strength, lady, and the ginger, by God, but not the knack, you understand. And we offered him a quieter little animal too. But what I say is, a bargain’s a bargain, that’s what I say. A bit dazed-like, sir, eh? My, you did come a cropper.”
“Sst! are you hurt?” I whispered.
The head shook; his moon-washed face smiled at me.
“Come now, come *now*,” I implored him, tugging at his arm, “before the crowd.﻿ ﻿…”
He recoiled as if my touch had scalded him.
“We go﻿—” I turned to the showman.
Hands thrust under his leathern belt, he looked fixedly at me, and then at the woman. Her eyes glittered glassily back at him.
“That’s it. The young lady knows best. He’s twisted his shoulder, lady; wrenched it; more weight than size, as you might say. She’ll know where to make her friend comfortable. Trust the ladies. Never you be afraid of that. Now, then, Mary, fetch up the gentleman’s cart.”
The woman, with one wolfish glance into his face, obeyed.
“There, sir! Is that easier? Push the rags in there behind his back. It’ll save the jolts. Lord love you, I wouldn’t split on the pair of you, not me. I know the old, old story. There, that’s it! Now, then, your ladyship. No more weight in the hand than a mushroom!

===Chinese===

人类嘲弄的声音是不会听错的。那一下残忍的拧绞，就在心口、在肋骨底下，也是不会错认的。我在原地打着旋跳了起来，一阵晕眩。
吼声沉下去了。一阵不分青红皂白的喧闹炸开——拍手的，跺脚的，吹哨的，喝倒彩的，嘘的，猫叫的，而这些又几乎全被铙钹、鼓和长号淹没：《再见，爱人，再见》。结束了。同莫纳里太太不一样，这帮乌合之众是不大容易满足的。可一切都好。那头大象——沉稳不可撼动的——那头携着手摇琴的睿智的大象，此刻该摇摇摆摆进场了。
我跑过践踏过的草地，去迎那走近来的一伙——班主、吉普赛女人、还有那匹发着抖、冒着汗的矮马。骑手俯身伏在鞍上，攥着鞍头，仿佛怕跌下来。他撑身下马，踉跄了几步，抬起手臂又垂下，想抚一抚那乳白的、咬着空气的口鼻，却没够着。斗篷的系带早断了。他从斗篷底下侧身挣出来，用左手笨拙地抹去脸上的尘土和湿汗。
「他还差着点儿诀窍，」班主正解释着。「马镫兴许短了一丁点儿。力气嘛，太太，还有那股猛劲儿，天知道，就是没诀窍，您明白。我们还备了匹性子稳当点儿的呢。可我这个人讲：买卖就是买卖，我就这话。有点儿发懵是不是，先生，呃？嚯，您可实实在在栽了个跟头。」
「嘘！伤着没有？」我悄声问。
他摇摇头；月光洗过的脸朝我微笑。
「这就走，这就*走*，」我拽着他的手臂恳求，「趁人还没围上来。……」
他猛地缩回手，仿佛我的触碰烫了他。
「我们走——」我转向班主。
班主双手插在皮腰带底下，定定看看我，又看看那女人。她的眼睛朝他亮晶晶地瞪回去。
「这就对了。还是小姐最明白。他扭了肩膀，太太；拧的；俗话说的，个头不大分量沉。该把朋友安顿在哪儿，她自有数。信太太们没错。这您只管放心。好嘞，玛丽，去把先生的马车牵来。」
那女人狼也似地朝他脸上扫了一眼，照办了。
「好，先生！这可松快点？把破布塞到他背后。颠簸能轻些。老天爱您，俺可不会出卖你们俩，俺不干那事儿。这种老掉牙的故事俺见多了。得，这就成了！好，小姐您的。手上轻得跟朵蘑菇似的！

===Original===

All serene, Mary. Home sweet home; that’s the tune, sir, ain’t it? Drive easy now: and off we go.”

===Chinese===

「一路太平，玛丽。家呀甜蜜的家——就是这支曲儿吧，先生，是不是？慢慢赶车：咱们这就走喙。」

### LIII / 五十三
===Original===

Noiselessly turned the wheels in the grass. We were descending the hill. A jolt, and we were in the road. A hedgerow shut us out from the two shrouded watchers by the tent. The braying music fainted away; and apart from the trotting hoofs and the grinding of the wheels in the dust, the only sound I heard was an occasional lofty crackle in space, as a rocket﻿—our last greeting from the circus﻿—stooping on its fiery course, strewed its coloured stars into the moonlight. Then the rearing hillside shut us out.
Speechlessly, from the floor of the cart, I watched the stooping figure above me. Ever and again, at any sudden lurch against a stone, he shrank down, then slowly lifted himself, turned his head and smiled.
“That’s the tune, sir; that’s the tune, sir.” The words aimlessly repeated themselves in my brain, as if bringing me a message I could not grasp or understand. “What was I thinking about?” a voice kept asking me. A strange, sluggish look dwelt in the dilated pupils under the drooping lids when the moonbeams struck in on us from between the branches. His right hand hung loosely down. I clasped it﻿—stone-cold.
“Listen, tell me,” I entreated, “you fell? I heard them calling, and﻿—and the clapping, what then?” I could speak no louder, but he seemed scarcely able to hear me.
“My shoulder,” he answered thickly, as if the words came sluggishly and were half-strange to him. “I fell.﻿ ﻿… Nothing: nothing. Only that I love you.”
The breath sighed itself away. I leaned my cheek against the unanswering hand, and chafed it with mine. Where now? Where now?
“We must keep awake,” I called beguilingly into the slumbrous face, after a long silence, as if to a child. “Awake!”
A sigh, as he smiled in answer, shook him from head to foot.
“You are thirsty? What’s this on your coat? Look, there is a gate. I’ll creep through and get help.” I scrambled up, endeavouring in vain to clutch at the reins.
But no; his head stirred its No; the left hand still held them fast. “Only﻿ ﻿… wait.”
*Was* it “wait”﻿—that last faint word? It fell into my mind like a leaf into a torrent, and before I could be sure of it, the sound was gone.

===Chinese===

车轮在草上无声地转。我们正下山。一颠，便上了大路。一道树篱，把帐篷旁那两个裹着罩衣的守望者隔在了我们身后。喧闹的乐声淡去；除了嘚嘚的蹄声和轮子碾尘的磨响，我听见的唯一声响，是空中偶尔一声高高的爆裂——一支焰火，马戏班对我们的最后致意——俯冲下它火红的弹道，把彩色的星子撒进月光。随后，高耸的山坡把我们掩没了。
我坐在车板上，无声地望着上方那俯身的身影。每逢车轮猛地磕上石头，他便一缩，随即又缓缓直起来，回过头，笑一笑。
“就是这个调子，先生；就是这个调子，先生。”这几个字在我脑子里无目的地翻来覆去，仿佛捎来一封我抓不住、也读不懂的信。“我在想来着？”一个声音一遍遍问我。月光从枝隙间打进车来时，我看见他低垂的眼睑下，放大的瞳孔里驻着一种奇怪的、迟滞的神情。他的右手松松垂着。我攋住它——冷得像石头。
“听着，告诉我，”我恳求，“你摔了？我听见他们喊，还——还有鼓掌，然后呢？”我的声音再也高不上去，可他似乎也几乎听不见我。
“我的肩膀，”他含混地答，字句仿佛来得迟缓，于他自己也半是陌生。“我摔了。……没什么：没什么。只是，我爱你。”
那口气叹息着自己散了。我把脸颊贴上那只不再回攋的手，用我的手搓着它。如今去哪里？如今去哪里？
“咱们得醒着，”长长一阵沉默后，我像哄孩子似的，往那张睡意沉沉的脸上轻唤。“醒着！”
他微笑作答，一声叹息把他从头到脚撆了一遍。
“你渴吗？你外衣上这是什么？瞧，那儿有道门。俺爬过去求援。”我手忙脚乱地起身，去够缰绳，够不着。
可不；他的头摆了摆它的“不”；左手仍把缰绳攋得死紧。“只……等等。”
那*是*“等等”吗——那最后一丝微弱的声音？它落进我心里，像一片叶落进激流，我还没来得及认准，声响已经没了。

===Original===

Instinct, neither his nor mine, guided us on through the winding lanes, up hill and down, along the margin of sleeping wood and light-dappled stream, over a level crossing whose dew-rusted rails gleamed in the moon, then up once more, the retreating hillside hollowly echoing to every clap of hoof against stone. There was no strength or will left in me, only thoughts which in the dark within, between waking and sleeping, seemed like hovering flies to veer and dart﻿—fantasies, fragments of dream, rather than thoughts.
I realized how sorely he was hurt, yet not then in my stupidity and horror﻿—or is it that I refused to confess it to myself?﻿—that his hurt was mortal. Morning would come soon. I grasped tight the hand in mine. Then help. In this monotony and weariness of mind and body, the passing trees seemed to dance and gesticulate before my eyes. A torturing drowsiness crept over me which in vain, thrusting up my eyelids with my fingers, beating my senseless feet on the floor of the cart, I tried to dispel. Once, I remember, I rose and threw my cape over his shoulder. At last I must have slept.
For the next thing I became conscious of was that the cart was at a standstill, and that the pony stood cropping the thyme-sweet turf by the wayside. I touched the cold dark hand. “Hush, my dear, we are here!”
But I expected no answer. The head was sunken between the heavy shoulders; the pallid features were set in an empty stare. There wasn’t a sound in the whole world, far or near. “Oh, but you haven’t said a single word to me!” It was the only speech in my mind﻿—a reproach. It died on my lips; I drew away. What was this?﻿—a dreadful fear plucked at my sleeve, fear of the company I was in, of a solitude never so much as tasted before. I leapt out of the cart, stood up in the dust, and in the creeping light stared about me.
Every window of the creeper-hung cottage was shrouded, its gate latched. I struggled to climb the fence, to fling a stone through the casement. The moon shone glassily in the cold skies, but daybreak was in the east; I must wait till morning. With eyes fixed on the motionless head I sat down in the grass by the wayside. Ever and again, after solemnly turning to survey me, the pony dragged the cart on a foot or two under the willows, nibbling the dewy grass.
Roused suddenly from stupor by the howling of a dog, I leapt up. Who called? Where was I?

===Chinese===

一种本能——既非他的，也非我的——引着我们穿行在蜿蜒的小巷里，上坡下坡，沿着沉睡的树林和光影斑驳的溪流边缘，越过一道平交道口——露水锈的铁轨在月下闪光——然后再度上坡，节节后退的山坡，把每一次蹄铁磕石的脆响空空地送回来。我身上再没有力气或意志，只剩念头——在内里的黑暗中，在醒与睡之间，它们像盘旋的苍蝇，忽转忽掠——与其说是念头，不如说是幻影、梦的碎片。
我明白他伤得有多重，却还没有——在我那愚钝与惊惶里——或者，是我拒绝向自己承认？——明白他的伤是致命的。早晨快来了。我紧紧攋住手里那只手。然后就得救了。在这身心两乏的单调里，掠过的树仿佛在我眼前起舞、比划。一种折磨人的睡意爬上我，我用手指撑起眼皮，用失去知觉的脚在车板上乱蹬，都驱它不走。记得有一次，我站起来，把披肩撞上他的肩头。最后，我一定是睡着了。
因为我再一有知觉时，车已停住，矮马正立在路旁，啃着百里香清甜的草皮。我碰碰那只又冷又暗的手。“嘘，亲爱的，我们到了！”
可我并不指望回答。头已沉进厚厚的肩膀之间；苍白的面容凝成一副空茫茫的注视。整个世界，远远近近，没有一点声音。“哦，可你连一句话都还没对我说呀！”我脑子里只剩这一句——一句埋怨。它死在我唇边；我缩了回来。这是什么？——一种骇人的恐惧扯住我的衣袖：怕我身边的这个同伴，怕一种我从未尝过的孤独。我跳下车，立在尘土里，在悄悄爬升的光线中环顾四周。
那座爬满藤蔓的村舍，扇扇窗都遮着，门拴着。我挣扎着想爬上篱笆，想丢块石头进窗。冷天里月亮照得像玻璃，东方却已有破晓；我只好等到天亮。我坐在路旁草里，眼睛定在那颗一动不动的头上。矮马隔一阵便庄严地回头审视我一回，再把车拖上一两英尺，到柳荫下啃沾露的草。
一声狗嗥把我从木然里骤然惊醒，我跳起来。谁在叫？我在哪里？

===Original===

What had I forgotten? In renewed and dreadful recognition I looked vacantly around me. A strangeness had come. His company was mine no longer.
Dawn brightened. The voice of a thrush pealed out of the orchard beyond the stone wall﻿—wild and sweet as in Spring. I crouched on the ground, elbows on knees, and now kept steady watch upon those night-hung upper windows. At last a curtain was drawn aside. An invisible face within must have looked down upon us in the lane. The casement was unlatched and thrust open, and a grey, tousled head pushed out as if in alarm into the keen morning. At sight of it a violent hiccuping seized me, so that when an old woman appeared at her door and hobbled out to the cart, I could not make myself understood. Her sleep-bleared, faded eyes surveyed me with horror and suspicion﻿—as if in my smallness there I looked scarcely human. She shook her crooked fingers at me, to scare me off; then stooping, put her head into the cart. I cried out, and ran﻿—

===Chinese===

我忘了什么？在重新袭来的、骇人的领悟里，我茫然四顾。一种陌生降临了。他的陪伴，不再是我的了。
天色亮开了。石墙那边的果园里，一只歌鸫放声唱起——狂野而甜美，一如春日。我蜷在地上，手肘支膝，目不转睛地守着那几扇还垂着夜幕的楼上窗。终于，一幅窗帘拉开了。屋里一张看不见的脸，必定正俯视着巷中的我们。窗闩一响，窗扇推开，一颗灰白蓬乱的脑袋探出来，仿佛惊惶地扎进凛冽的清晨。一看见它，一阵剧烈的打嗝攋住了我，以致当一位老妇人出现在门口、蹒跚着朝大车走来时，我说的话她一个字也听不懂。她那睡眼惺忪、褪了色的眼睛惊惧而狐疑地打量我——仿佛我这般小地立在彼处，几乎不似人形。她朝我晃着弯曲的手指，要吓走我；随后弯下腰，把头探进车里。我大叫一声，跑了——

### LIV / 五十四
===Original===

The sun had burned for some hours in the heavens, when bleeding with thorns and on fire with nettles and stinking mayweed, I dragged myself out of the undergrowth into a low-lying corner of the desolate garden. Near by lay a pool of water under an old ruinous wall, swept by the foliage of an ash. On a flat, shelving stone at its brink I knelt down, bathed my face, and drank.
All that day I spent in the neighbourhood of the water, overhung with the colourless trumpets of convolvulus. Occasionally I edged on, but only to keep pace with the sunbeams, for I was deathly cold, and as soon as shadow drew over me, fits of shivering returned. For some hours I slept, but so shallowly that I heard my own voice gabbling in dreams.
When I awoke, the western sky was an ocean of saffron and gold. Amidst its haze, stood up the distant clustered chimneys of Wanderslore: and I realized I must be in an outlying hollow of the park﻿—farthest from Beechwood Hill. I sat up, bound back my hair, and, bathing my swollen feet in the dark, ice-cold water, I watched the splendour fade.
While there was still light in the sky I set out for the cottage again, but soon found myself in such distress amongst the tangled weeds and grasses, which at every movement flung their stifling dust and seeds and pollen over me, that I was compelled to give up the attempt. With senseless tears dropping down my cheeks, I returned to the pool, and made my bed in the withered bracken.
So passed the next days. When once more the cloudless heat of the sun had diminished, I made another attempt to press back by the way I had come, if only to look up at those windows again. But I was dazed and exhausted; lost my way; and, keeping watch until daybreak, I returned again to the pool. Sitting there, I tried to control my misery and be calm. “Wait, wait; I am coming,” was my one inarticulate thought. Surely that other solitude must be the easier to bear. But it was in vain. He was dead; and I had killed him﻿—pride, vanity, greed, obstinacy, lovelessness. Every flower and fading leaf bore witness against me.
Now and again I quenched my thirst and rambled off a little way in search of a few fallen hazel nuts and blackberries, and attempted to ease the pain and distress I was in. But I knew in my heart that a few such days must see the last of me, and I had no other desire. Evening came with its faint stars.

===Chinese===

日头在天上已烧了几个钟头，我带着荆棘划破的伤口、被荨麻和臭甘菊烧灼着，从灌木丛里拖出自己，爬进荒园一角低洼的所在。近旁一堵残墙下卧着一泓池水，白蜡树的枝叶在上面拂扫。我在水边一块平斜的石上跪下，洗了脸，喝了水。
那一整天，我都守在水边，头顶悬着旋花无色的喇叭。偶尔我挪动一下，也只为跟上阳光的脚步——因为我冷得要死，影子一罩上我，阵阵寒颤便卷土重来。我睡了几个钟头，却睡得极浅，浅得听见自己的声音在梦里咭咭呱呱。
醒来时，西天是一片藏红与黄金的海洋。雾霭之中，耸着旺德斯洛远处成簇的烟囱：我明白了，我必是身在园子最偏的一处洼地里——离山毛榉林山最远的一隅。我坐起身，绾起头发，把肿胀的双足浸进幽暗冰凉的水里，望着那片壮丽褪尽。
趁天上还有光，我又向那村舍进发，可很快就陷入缠结的野草荒榛之间，苦不堪言——每动一步，它们便把呛人的尘土、草籽和花粉劈头盖脸掷来——只得罢手。麻木的泪珠滚下面颊，我回到池边，在枯蕨里铺了我的床。
接下来的几天就这样过去。待无云的骄阳再度敛威，我又试图沿来路折返，哪怕只求再仰头望一眼那些窗。可我神思恍惚，气力耗竭；迷了路；提心吊胆挨到天明，又回到池边。坐在那里，我竭力按住悲惨，装出平静。“等着，等着；我就来了，”是我唯一一句不成声的念头。那种别样的孤寂，想必总要好受些。可全是徒然。他死了；是我杀了他——骄傲、虚荣、贪心、执拗、无爱。每一朵花、每一片凋叶，都出言指证我。
我不时解解渴，蹒跚着走开一小段，寻几颗落地的榛子和黑莓，想缓一缓周身的痛楚与窘迫。可我心里明白，这样的日子再来几天，便要送走我最后的一口气，而我别无所愿。黄昏携着疏星来了。

===Original===

My mind at last seemed to empty itself of thought; and until dark fell, a self sat at the windows of my eyes gazing heedlessly out over that peace and beauty without consciousness even of grief and despair. Nocturnal creatures began to stir in weed and thicket; a thin mist to rise. For a while I kept watch until sense left me, and I slept.
A waning misshapen moon hung over the garden when I awoke, my mind still, clear, empty. So empty that I might but just have reentered the world after the lapse of ages. In this silvery hush of night, winged shapes were wheeling around and above me, piercing the air with mad, strident cries. With sight strangely sharpened and powerful, I gazed tranquilly up, and supposed for a while these birds were swallows. Idly I watched them, scarcely conscious whether they were real or creatures of the imagination.
Darting, swooping in the mild blaze of the moonlight, with gaping beaks and whirring wings, they swept, wavered, tumbled above their motionless pastures; ghostly-fluttering, feathery-plumed moths their prey. At last, a continuous churring, like the noise of a rattle, near at hand, betrayed them. I lay in my solitude in the midst of a whirling flock of nightjars, few in number, but beside themselves with joy, on the eve of their autumnal flight.
I can only grope my way now through vague and baffling memories. Maybe it was the frenzied excitement of these madly happy birds that shed itself into my defenceless mind, after rousing me into the night I knew too well. With full, vigilant eyes I am standing again a few paces from the brink of the pool, looking up into a moonlit bush of deadly nightshade, its noxious flowering over, and hung with its black, gleaming, cherry-like fruit. I cannot recall having ever given a thought to this poisonous plant in Wanderslore during my waking hours, though in my old happy reconnoitrings of the garden I had sometimes chanced on the coral-red clusters of the woody nightshade﻿—the bittersweet, and had afterwards seen it in blossom.
It may be that only a part of my mind was fully awake, while the rest dreamed on.

===Chinese===

我的心终于仿佛把念头倒空了；天黑之前，一个“我”坐在眼睛的窗后，浑然不觉悲、不觉绝望，茫茫然望着那片安宁与美。夜行的生灵开始在草莽与棘丛里骚动；薄雾升起。我守望了一阵，直到知觉离我而去，睡去。
再醒来时，一弯残缺畸形的月悬在园子上空，我的心静止、清朗、空空。空得仿佛历经万古，我才重新入世。夜的银色静谧里，有翼的影子绕着我、在我头顶盘旋，以疯狂、尖锐的鸣声刺破空气。我的视力出奇地锐利有力，平静地仰望上去，有一阵还当那些鸟是燕子。我懒懒望着它们，几乎分不清它们是真是心中的造物。
它们在月光温润的光焰里疾掠、俯冲，张着喙，振翅嗡嗡，在纹丝不动的牧场上空扫荡、摇曳、翻滚；猎物是那些幽灵般扑闪、羽状翅的蛾子。终于，近旁一阵连续的“轧轧”声，像响板般的聒噪，出卖了它们。我躺在孤独里，身处一群回旋飞舞的夜鹰之中——为数不多，却欢喜得忘乎所以——正当它们秋徙前夜。
如今我只能凭着模糊难解的记忆摸索前行。也许是这些狂喜之鸟的癫狂兴奋，把我唤醒进那个我太熟悉的夜之后，又倾洒进我不设防的心。我又站在离池岸几步远的地方，睁着圆圆的、警醒的眼，仰望月光下一丛颠茄——有毒的花期已过，枝头垂着黑亮、樱桃似的浆果。我不记得清醒时可曾留意过旺德斯洛里的这种毒物，虽说在旧日快活的园中踏勘里，我偶尔撞见过欧白英珊瑚红的果串——那“苦甜藤”——后来也见过它开花。
也许，我的心只有一角全然醒着，其余部分还在梦。

===Original===

Yet, as I strive to return in imagination to that solitary hour, I am certain that a complete realization was mine of the power distilled into those alluring light-glossed berries; and, slave of my drowsy senses, I fixed gaze and appetite on them as though, from childhood up, they had been my one greed and desire. Even then, as if for proof that they were real, my eyes wandered; recognized, low in the west, glaring Altair amid the faint outspread wings of Aquila; pondered on the spark-like radiance struck out by the moonbeams from the fragments of tile that protruded here and there from the crumbling wall beyond the pool; and softly returned once more to the evil bush.
Then, for an instant, I fancied that out of the nearer shadows a half-seen form had stolen up close behind me, and was watching me. Fancy or not, it caused me no fear. I turned about where I stood, and from this gentle eminence scanned the immense autumnal garden with its coursing night-birds and distant motionless woods. No; I was alone; by myself; conscious only of an unfathomable quiet; and I stooped and took up one of the ripe fruits that had fallen to the ground. “Ah, ah!” called a faraway voice within me. “Ah, ah! What are you at now?”﻿—a voice like none I had ever heard in the world until that moment. Yet I raised the fruit to my lips.
Its bitter juices jetted out upon cheek, mouth, and tongue, forever staining me with their dye. Their very rancour shocked my body wide awake. Struck suddenly through with frightful cold and terror, I flung the vile thing down, and scoured my mouth with the draggled hem of my skirt. “Oh God! oh God!” I cried; then turned, ran a few steps, tripped, turned back and cast myself down, crushing my eyes with my hands; and in helpless confusion began to pray.
Minutes, hours, passed﻿—I know not. But at last, with throat parched and swollen, and hands and cheeks and scalp throbbing with an unnatural heat, I raised my eyes. Two moons were in the sky, hideously revolving amid interwoven arcs of coloured light, and running backward and forward. I called out in the silence. A gigantic nightjar swirled on me, plucking at my hair. A maddening vertigo seized me. I went stumbling and staggering down to my stone and drenched head and breast in the flashing black and silver water.
It was a momentary refreshment, and in its influence memory began droning of the past.

===Chinese===

然而，当我竭力在想象中重返那孤独的时刻，我确知：那些光泽诱人的浆果里蒸馏出的力量，我当时是完全明了的；而我，成了昏沉感官的奴隶，把目光和馋欲都钉在它们上头，仿佛自幼年起它们便是我唯一的贪念与渴望。即便那样，像是为了求证它们是真，我的眼睛也曾游移；在西天低处，认出了天鹰座淡淡舒展的双翼间那颗灼灼的河鼓二；端详月光从池那边残墙间处处探出的碎瓦上击出的火花般的光芒；然后又软软地回到那丛恶灌木上。
随后，有一瞬，我恍惚觉得近处的暗影里溜出一个半明半昧的身影，潜到我背后，正注视我。是真是幻，都吓不着我。我在原地转过身，从这道温缓的高地上扫视无垠的秋园——夜鸟疾飞，远处林木凝然不动。不；我独自一人；只我一个人；只觉出一种无底的寂静；我俯身拾起一颗落在地上的熟果。“啊，啊！”我体内一个遥远的声音唤道。“啊，啊！你这是在做什么？”——那嗓音，此前我在世上从未听过。可我还是把果子举到了唇边。
苦汁喷射到我的脸颊、口腔和舌上，用它的染料把我永远渍污了。那股烈烈的苦恶，把我周身激得彻底清醒。一阵彻骨的寒与恐怖蓦地穿透我，我把那可憎的东西摔在地上，用湿拖的裙裾猛擦嘴。“哦上帝！哦上帝！”我喊；随即转身，跑了几步，绊倒，又折回来扑倒在地，双手死死压住眼睛；在无措的慌乱里开始祷告。
几分钟，几小时，过去了——我不知多久。终于，喉咙干肿，手、颊和头皮随着一股不自然的热突突跳着，我抬起了眼。天上有两轮月亮，在交织的彩色光弧间可怖地旋转，忽前忽后。我在寂静里喊出声。一只巨大的夜鹰朝我盘旋扑来，扯我的头发。一阵令人发狂的眩晕攋住我。我跌跌撞撞挪到我的石头上，把头和胸口浸进黑银闪烁的水里。
那只是一晌的清凉；在它的余荫里，记忆开始嗡嗡地低诉往昔。

===Original===

Confused abhorrent images mocked my helpless dreamings. There was a place﻿—beyond﻿—out of these shadows, unattainable. A piercing, vindictive voice was calling me. No hope now. I was damned. In senseless hallucination I began systematically, laboriously, a frenzied search. Leaf, pebble, crawling night-creature﻿—with slow, animal-like care, I turned them over one by one, seeking and seeking.

===Chinese===

混乱而可憎的影像，嘲弄我无助的梦。有一个地方——在彼岸——在这些暗影之外，不可企及。一个尖利的、挟怨的声音在唤我。如今没有指望了。我遭了天罚。在失去知觉的幻觉里，我开始了一场有条不紊、艰苦卓绝、疯狂至极的搜寻。叶片、卵石、爬行的夜虫——我用动物般迟缓的细心，把它们一一翻过来，寻啊，寻啊。

## London / 伦敦
===Original===



===Chinese===

（伦敦）

### LV / 五十五
===Original===

And yet again I pause﻿—long after these last words were written﻿—to look back across the intervening years at that young woman. What, indeed, was her insane mind seeking: what assurance, reconciliation? I know not, but there she herself was found, nails worn to the quick, feet shoeless, a hunted anatomy. Her fret and fever were to pass away; but what has all this experience done for me?﻿—that wildest, happiest, cruellest, dearest, blackest twelvemonth of my life? One more unanswerable question. But, thank God, I live on; have even finished the task I set myself; and in spite of fits and moods of depression, distaste, and weariness, have been happy in it. Even when most contemptuous and ashamed of myself, I have still found comfort in the belief that truth is a wholesome medicine, though in essence it be humanly unattainable. And my work has taught me this too﻿—not to fret so foolishly as once I did, at being small and insignificant in body; to fear a great deal more remaining pygmy-minded, and pygmy-spirited. I used to try to set myself against the World﻿—but no need to enter further into that. We *cannot* see ourselves as others see us, but that is no excuse for not wearing spectacles; and even up here, in my peaceful lonely old Stonecote, I must beware of a mind swept and garnished. Moreover my hour must come again: and his.
That being so, of this I am certain; that it will be impossible to free myself, to escape from this world, unless in peace and amity I can take every shred of it, every friend and every enemy, all that these eyes have seen, these senses discovered with me. I *know* that. And perhaps for that very reason, in spite of the loving gratitude that overcomes me at the thought of what my existence might have been, I sometimes dread the ease and quiet and seclusion in which I live. And this tale itself? As Mrs. Monnerie had said, what is it but once more to have drifted into being on show again﻿—in a book? That is so; and so I must leave it, hoping against hope that one friend at any rate will consent in his love and wisdom to take me seriously, and to remember me, not with scorn or even with pity, but as if, life for life, we had shared the world on equal terms.
M.

===Chinese===

而这些字写就许久之后，我又一次停笔——回望隔在中间的那些年，望向那个年轻女子。她那颗疯狂的头脑，究竟在寻找什么：什么担保，什么和解？我不知道。可她自己，就在那里被人寻见：指甲磨秃见肉，双脚无鞋，一副被追猎的骸骨。她的焦灼与热病终将过去；可这一番经历，又为我留下了什么？——我那一生中最狂放、最幸福、最残酷、最亲爱、最黑暗的十二个月？又一个无从作答的问题。但感谢上帝，我还活着；甚至完成了我自己定下的功课；纵有阵阵的消沉、厌倦与疲怠，我在其中仍是幸福的。哪怕最鄙夷自己、最羞惭的时候，我也仍能从这一信念里得安慰：真相是一剂良药，尽管它本质上非人力所能企及。这份功课还教会我——不再像我从前那样，为身体的细小卑微愚魯地焦心；倒是更怕心智侏儒、性灵侏儒得多。我从前总想同这世界对着干——那就不必多说了。我们*不可能*像旁人看我们那样看见自己，可这并不是不戴眼镜的借口；况且哪怕在这高处的、我安宁孤寂的老斯通科特，我也得提防一颗打扫得空空荡荡、装点得体体面面的心。何况，我的时辰必会再来：他的也是。
既然如此，这一点我便确信：若不能在平和与亲睦中携上这世界的一丝一缕——每一位朋友、每一位仇敌、这双眼睛见过的一切、这些感官同我一道发现的一切——我便不可能脱身，不可能逃离这个世界。这我*知道*。也许正因如此，一想到我的存在本可能何等模样，感激与爱便涌上心头；可有时，我又惧怕我此刻所享的安闲、静谧与幽居。而这一篇故事呢？正如莫纳里太太所说：它算什么，不过是又一次漂流到被观看的境地——在一本书里？确是如此；那我就这样把它留下，怀着无望之望：至少还有一位朋友，肯以他的爱与智慧把我当真，肯记起我——不带轻蔑，甚至也不带怜悯，而是仿佛，生命对生命，我们曾以平等的身分共享过这个世界。
M.

## Monks’ House / 僧侣宅
===Original===



===Chinese===

僧侣宅

### V / V
===Original===

Am I sorry that almost beside myself with this new affliction, and bewildered and frightened by the incessant coming and going of strangers in the house, I refused to be carried down to bid that unanswering face goodbye? No, I have no regret on that score. The older I grow the more closely I seem to understand him. If phantoms of memory have any reality﻿—and it is wiser, I think, to remember the face of the living rather than the stony peace of the dead﻿—he has not forgotten his only daughter.
Double-minded creature I was and ever shall be; now puffed up with arrogance at the differences between myself and gross, common-sized humanity; now stupidly sensitive to the pangs to which by reason of these differences I have to submit. At times I have been tempted to blame my parents for my shortcomings. What wicked folly﻿—they did not choose their only child. After all, too, fellow creatures of any size seem much alike. They rarely have *nothing* to blame Providence for﻿—the length of their noses or the size of their feet, their bones or their corpulence, the imbecilities of their minds or their bodies, the “accidents” of birth, breeding, station, or circumstance. Yet how secure and perhaps wholesome is Man’s self-satisfaction. To what ideal does he compare himself but to a self-perfected abstraction of his own image? Even his Venus and Apollo are mere flattering reflections of his own he- or she-shapes. And what of his anthropomorphic soul?
As for myself, Dame Nature may some day take a fancy to the dwarf. “What a pretty play it would be”﻿—I have clean forgotten where I chanced on this amusing passage﻿—“What a pretty play it would be if, from the next generation onwards, the only humans born into the world should be of mere pygmy stature. Fifty years hence there would remain but few of the normal-sized in the land. Imagine these aged few, miserably stalking through the dwarfed streets, picking up a scanty livelihood in city or countryside, where their very boots would be a public danger, their very tread would set the bells in the steeples ringing, and their appetites would be a national incubus. House, shop, church, high road, furniture, vehicles abandoned or sunken to the pygmy size; wars and ceremonies, ambitions and enterprises, everything but prayers, dwindled to the petty.

===Chinese===

这新的打击几乎令我失魂落魄，家里陌生人来来往往、川流不息，又叫我惶惑惊惧，于是我拒绝让人抱下楼去，同那张再无应答的脸诀别——为此我可懊悔吗？不，这方面我无所憾。年岁越长，我仿佛越贴近地懂得他。倘若记忆的幻影尚有几分真实——而且我想，记住生者的容颜，总比记住死者那石头的安宁更明智——那么，他并没有忘掉他唯一的女儿。
我是个两心的人，从前是，永远也是；一时因自己同粗蠢的常人之间的差异而傲气鼓胀；一时又因这些差异使我不得不承受的痛楚而愚蠢地敏感。有时我禁不住要怨父母给我的这些短处。多么邪恶的糊涂——他们又没有挑选过他们唯一的孩子。说到底，无论什么尺码的同类，看来都相差无几。他们很少*没有*什么可埋怨造物的——鼻子的长短呀，脚的大小呀，骨头呀，肥瘦呀，心智或身体的低能呀，出身、教养、门第、境遇的「意外」呀。然而人的自我满足是多么安稳，说不定还挺有益。他拿什么理想来比量自己呢？无非是他自己形象的一幅自我完善的抽象。连他的维纳斯和阿波罗，也不过是他男形女态的谄媚倒影。那么他那按自己的模样造就的灵魂呢？
至于我自己，自然夫人说不定哪天会看中侏儒。「那将是多好玩的一出戏」——这段妙文是在哪儿偶然读到的，我已忘得干干净净——「那将是多好玩的一出戏，倘若从下一代起，降生到世上来的人类，个个都只有侏儒的身材。五十年后，国中身材正常的人便所剩无几了。想象一下这几位高龄者，凄凄惶惶地穿行在侏儒的街巷间，在城市或乡间拾掇一点微薄的生计：他们那双靴子便是公共的危险，他们一抬脚便叫教堂尖塔上的钟齐鸣，他们的胃口便是全国的梦魇。房屋、店铺、教堂、大道、家具、车辆，尽数废弃，或缩降为侏儒的尺寸；战争与典仪、野心与事业，一切一切，除了祷告，都萎缩成了琐碎。

===Original===

Would great-grandfather be venerated, cherished, admired, a welcome guest, a lamented emigrant? Would there be as many mourners as sextons at his funeral, as many wreaths as congratulations at his grave?” And so on and so forth﻿—like Jonathan Swift.
But I must beware. Partly from fatigue and partly from dislike of the version of Miss M. that stared out of his picture at me, I had begun, I remember, to be a little fretful when old Mr. Wagginhorne was painting my portrait. And I complained pertly that I thought there were far too many azaleas on the potted bush.
“Ah, little Miss Finical,” he said, “take care, if you please. Once there was a Diogenes whom the gods shut up in a tub and fed on his own spleen. He died.﻿ ﻿… He died,” he repeated, drawing his brush slowly along the canvas, “of dyspepsia.”
He popped round, “Think of that.”
I can think of that to better purpose now, and if there is one thing in the world whose company I shall deplore in my coffin, that thing is a Cynic. That is why I am trying as fast as I can to put down my experiences in black and white before the black predominates.
But I must get back to my story. My poor father had left his affairs in the utmost disorder. His chief mourners were his creditors. Apart from these, one or two old country friends and distant relatives, I believe, attended his funeral, but none even of them can have been profoundly interested in the Hop, the Oyster, or the Cherry, at least in the abstract. Dr. Grose, owing to ill-health, had given up his practice and was gone abroad. But though possibly inquiry was made after the small creature that had been left behind, I stubbornly shut myself away in my room under the roof, listening in a fever of apprehension to every sinister movement in the house beneath.
Yet if a friend in need is a friend indeed, then I must confess that my treatment of Miss Fenne was the height of ingratitude.
In my grief and desolation, the future seemed to be only a veil beyond the immediate present, which I had neither the wish nor the power to withdraw. Miss Fenne had no such illusions. I begged Pollie to make any excuse she could think of to prevent her from seeing me. But at last she pushed her way up, and doubtless, the news and the advice she brought were the best tonic that could have been prescribed for me.

===Chinese===

曾祖父会受人尊敬、疼爱、景仰么？会是个受欢迎的宾客、令人哀悼的远行者么？他的葬礼上，送葬的人会同掘墓人一样多么？他坟上，花圈会同贺词一样多么？」如此等等，不一而足——很有一番斯威夫特的笔意。
可我得小心。一部分出于疲惫，一部分出于厌恶画上那个瞪着我的M小姐（Miss M.）的版本，我记得，老瓦金霍恩先生（Mr. Wagginhorne）给我画像的时候，我已开始有点烦躁。我还放肆地抱怨说，盆里那丛杜鹃花未免开得太多。
「啊哈，挑剔的小姐，」他说，「请你当心。从前有个第欧根尼，众神把他关进一只木桶，拿他自己的怨气喂养他。他死了。……他死了，」他重复道，画笔在画布上缓缓拖过，「死于消化不良。」
他猛地转过身来：「想想这个吧。」
如今我能更有益地想想这个了；倘若世上有一样东西，躺在棺材里的我将为其相伴而悲叹，那东西就是愤世嫉俗者。正因如此，我才拼命赶着，趁黑还没占上风，把我的经历用白纸黑字记下来。
可我得回到我的故事上。我可怜的父亲把身后的事务掠得一团糟。他的主要送葬人是他的债主们。此外，我相信，一两个乡间故旧和远亲出席了他的葬礼，可就连他们，对「蛇麻」「牡蛎」或「樱桃」——至少抽象地看——也谈不上有多深的关切。格罗斯医生（Dr. Grose）因健康欠佳，已歇了诊，出国去了。虽然或许有人打听过遗下的这个小东西，我却执拗地把自己关在屋顶下的房间里，怀着热病般的忧惧，谛听着楼下宅中每一声不祥的动静。
然而，若说患难见真友，那我必须承认，我对芬恩小姐（Miss Fenne）的态度，实在是负义的极致。
在我的悲恸与孤寂里，未来不过是眼门前的一层帷幕，我既无意、也无力去揭开。芬恩小姐可没有这类幻觉。我央求波莉（Pollie）想出随便什么借口，拦住她别让她见我。可她终于还是挤上楼来，而毋庸置疑，她带来的消息与忠告，是能为我开出的最好的药方。

===Original===

As a child I had always associated my godmother with the crocodile (though not with Mr. Bosch’s charming conception of it, in his picture of the Creation). Yet there were no tears in her faded eyes when she explained that of my father’s modest fortune not a pittance remained. In a few days the house, with everything in it except my own small sticks of furniture, was to be sold by auction. I must keep my door locked against intruders. All that would be left to me was a small income of about £110 per annum, derived from money bequeathed to me by a relative of my mother’s whom I had never seen.
“I fancy your father knew nothing about it,” she concluded, “at least so your dear *mother* seemed to imply. But there! it’s a sad business, a sad business. And that Tapa scandal; a lamentable affair.” Having thus prepared the way, my godmother proposed that I should take up my residence in her house, and commit my future entirely to her charge.
“You cannot be an expensive guest,” she explained, “and I am sure you will try to be a grateful one. No truly *conscientious* godparent, my dear child, *ever* relinquishes the soul committed to her care. I sometimes wonder whether your poor dear mother realized this.”
But it was my soul, if that is brother to the spirit and can be neighbour to pride, that revolted against her proposition. I had to shut my eyes at the very remembrance of Miss Fenne’s prim and musty drawing-room. Every intimation, every jerk of her trembling head, every pounce of her jewelled fingers only hardened my heart. Poor Miss Fenne. Her resentment at my refusal seemed to increase her shortness of sight. Looking in on her from my balcony, I had the advantage of her, as she faced me in the full light in her chair, dressed up in her old lady’s clothes like a kind of human Alp among my pygmy belongings. I tried to be polite, but this only increased her vexation. One smart tap of the ivory ball that topped her umbrella would have been my coup de grâce. She eyed me, but never administered it.
At last she drew in her lips and fell silent. Then, as may happen at such moments, her ill-temper and chagrin, even the sense of her own dignity drooped away, and for a while in the quietness we were simply two ill-assorted human beings, helpless in the coils of circumstance.

===Chinese===

孩提时代，我总把教母同鳄鱼联想到一处（虽然不是同博斯先生在《创世》图里对鳄鱼的那番妙想）。可当她说明我父亲那份微薄的家产已所剩无几时，她那双褪了色的眼睛里并没有泪。几天之内，宅子和屋里的一切——除开我那几件小小的家具——都要拍卖。我必须锁好门，提防闯入者。留给我的，只有一笔小小的进项，每年约一百一十镑，出自母亲一位亲戚遗赠给我的钱，那位亲戚我从没见过。
「我想你父亲对此一无所知，」她总结道，「至少你亲爱的*母亲*话里似有此意。可是唉！这是件伤心事，伤心事。还有那桩塔帕丑闻；可叹，可叹。」如此铺垫停当，教母便提议我搬到她宅中去住，把我的前程全然托付给她照管。
「你当客人花不了几个钱，」她解释说，「而且我确信你会努力做一个知恩图报的客人。真正*尽责*的教亲，我亲爱的孩子，*从来*不放弃托付给她照看的灵魂。有时我怀疑，你那可怜的亲妈妈可明白这一点。」
可偏偏是我的灵魂——倘若它同灵性是手足，又能与自尊为邻——起来反抗她的提议。只要一想起芬恩小姐那间古板而霉味扑鼻的客厅，我就不得不闭上眼睛。她的每一句示意，她颤抖的脑袋的每一次抽动，她戴戒指的手指的每一次突戳，都只叫我的心更硬。可怜的芬恩小姐。遭我拒绝的怨愤，似乎更添了她的老眼昏花。我从阳台上居高临下地望她，占了便宜：她坐在全光亮处，一身老妇人的装束，在我的侏儒家什之间，像一座人形的阿尔卑斯山。我竭力以礼相待，却只添了她的恼怒。她那把伞顶的象牙球只需轻轻一敲，便足以给我致命一击。她盯视着我，却始终没有落下来。
末了她抿紧嘴唇，沉默了。随后，正如这种时刻常有的事，她的坏脾气与懊恼，连同她对自身尊严的自觉，都蒿了下去；有一阵子，在寂静里，我们不过是两个不般配的人，在境遇的缠缚里无能为力。

===Original===

She composed her mouth, adjusted her bonnet strings, peered a moment from dim old eyes out of the window, then once more looked at me.
“It must be, then, as God wills,” she said in a trembling voice. “The spirit of your poor dear mother must be judge between us. She has, we may trust, gone to a better world.”
For a moment my resolution seemed to flow away like water, and I all but surrendered. But a rook cawed close overhead, and I bit my lip. Little more was said, except that she would consider it her duty to find me a comfortable and God-fearing home. But she admonished me of the future, warned me that the world was a network of temptations, and assured me of her prayers. So we parted. I bowed her out of my domain. It was the last time we met. Two days afterwards I received her promised letter:﻿—

===Chinese===

她端正了嘴，理好帽带，用昏花的老眼朝窗外望了片刻，然后又看向我。
「那就，唯有听凭上帝的旨意了，」她声音颤抖地说。「只好让你那可怜的亲妈妈的在天之灵，来做我们之间的裁判。她——我们可以确信——已去了更好的世界。」
有一瞬间，我的决心仿佛流水般要泻走，我几乎就要降服。可一只白嘴鸦在头顶近处叫了一声，我咬住了嘴唇。此后话已不多，只说她将把为我寻一处安适而敬畏上帝的家视为己任。她训诫我以未来，警告我说这世界是诱惑织成的罗网，并向我保证她的祷告。我们就这样分手了。我鞠躬送她出了我的领地。那是我们最后一次见面。两天后，我收到了她应许的信：——

===Original===

> “**My Dear Godchild**﻿—Mr. Ambrose Pellew, an old *clergyman* friend of mine, in whose discretion and knowledge of the world I have every confidence, has spoken for you to an old married, respectable servant of his now living a few miles from London﻿—a Mrs. Bowater. For the charge of thirty shillings a week she has consented to give you board, lodging, and *reasonable* attendance. In all the circumstances this seems to me to be a moderate sum. Mr. Pellew assures me that Mrs. B. is clean, honest, and a *practising* Christian. When this dreadful Sale is over, I have arranged that Pollie shall conduct you safely to what will in future be your *home*. I trust that you will be as happy there as Providence permits, though I cannot doubt that your poor dear mother and your poor father, too, for that matter, would have wished otherwise﻿—that the roof of her old friend who was present at your Baptism and *insisted* on your Confirmation, should have been your refuge and asylum now that you are absolutely alone in the world.
> “However, you have rejected this proposal, and have *chosen your own path*. I am not your legal guardian, and I am too deeply *pained* to refer again to your obstinacy and ingratitude. Rest assured that, in spite of all, I shall remember you in my prayers, and I trust, D.V., that you will escape the temptations of this wicked world﻿—a world in which it has pleased God, in spite of self-sacrificing and anxious friends, to place you at so distressing a disadvantage. But in His Sight all men are equal. Let that be your continual consolation. See Amos 7:2; Prov. 31:24﻿–﻿28; Eccles. 12:1.
> “I remain, your affectionate godmother,
> “Emma E. Fenne.
> “P.S.﻿—I reopen this letter to explain that your *financial* affairs are in the hands of Messrs. Harris, Harris, and Harris, respectable solicitors of Gray’s Inn. They will remit you on every quarter day﻿—Christmas Day, Lady Day, June 25th and September 29th﻿—the sum of £28 10s. 0d. Of this you will pay £19 10s. *at once* to Mrs. Bowater, who, I have no doubt, will advise you on the expenditure of what remains on wearing apparel, self-improvement, missions, charity, and so on. It *grieves* me that from the wreckage of your father’s affairs you must not anticipate a further straw of assistance.

> 「**亲爱的教女**——安布罗斯·佩柳先生（Mr. Ambrose Pellew），我的一位*牧师*老友，其持重与阅历我素来深信不疑，已代你向他的一个年长已婚、品行端正的仆人问过了——就是现住在离伦敦几英里处的鲍沃特太太（Mrs. Bowater）。每周三十先令，她已应允供你膳宿及*适度的*照应。综观种种情形，我以为这是公道的数目。佩柳先生向我担保，鲍太太洁净、诚实，且是*身体力行*的基督徒。等这可怕的拍卖一了结，我已安排波莉把你平安送到你今后的*家*去。愿天意容你在那儿得享多少快乐，便享多少快乐；虽然我毫不怀疑，你那可怜的亲妈妈——还有你那可怜的爸爸，就此事而言——本会另有期望：如今你在世上孤身一人，本该由这位出席过你洗礼、又*力主*你行坚振礼的老朋友的屋顶，来作你的庇护与收容。
